notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg4036.tlg001.opp-grc1: A gap of about 15 letters follows 'insensible' (ἀναισθητεῖν προσ . . . γραφόντων); the words around it cannot be construed. 'τῶν προκειμένων θεαμάτων τὸν ἀγαθοειδῆ βούλησιν' looks corrupt and is translated loosely ('for the spectacles set before him, the man of good form, by [divine] will'). μενον after προστησάμενον is a dittography. ἀγγελικὴ τάξις, 'messenger's office', also means 'angelic rank'. παρέχονται is taken as παραδέχονται, 'receive'; the editor's † marks a corruption in the following clause. At the end τὴν θείαν is taken with an implied 'vision'.
φανταζομένων is printed twice (a dittography) and translated once. 'ἐν σχήμασιν ἄλλοτε' seems to lack a word ('now in one shape, now in another'). προισέμενοι = προϊέμενοι.

nodes.text: These things having been demonstrated by Plato, with regard to the first [type] the difficulty is raised: where do evils come from? For if they come from god, the argument that shows the divine to be the cause of good things only is false; if from elsewhere, then if that [source] is from god, the divine is all the more the cause of evils; but if it is not from god, the principles are more than one, one of goods and the other of evils. With regard to the second: how do the self-manifestations of the gods come about, when at one time unshaped lights appear, at another shaped ones? For if we do not admit these, we overturn the whole hieratic art and the works of the theurgists, and, apart from these, the spontaneous epiphanies of the gods, who appear at different times in [different] shapes. So it is a puzzle how something divine, which does not change, is seen in person in different forms. With regard to the third: how are false oracles given, when those who give the oracles do not lie — oracles of which all the oracular shrines are full? And how, since the good is prior to truth, will the gods not, for the sake of the good, sometimes lie and deceive those unworthy to attain the truth directly? These are the difficulties one might raise against the arguments stated, although they have been proved from necessary [premises].

We shall be right to say that Er's return to life was nothing other than the entry into the body of the soul that had been separated from it; for its *bios* [life lived in a body] is its common life with the body; the recovery of this, then, he called *anabiōsis* [return to bios], since it is a change from its own proper life to the common and composite one. That the soul can both go out of the body and come into it is shown also by the man in Clearchus who used the soul-drawing wand on the sleeping youth, and who persuaded the divine Aristotle, as Clearchus says in his books On Sleep, about the soul: that it is separated from the body, that it enters into the body, and that it uses it as a kind of lodging. For striking the boy with the wand, he drew out his soul, and, as it were leading it by means of the wand far from the body, he showed that the body was motionless and, though kept unharmed, insensible [...] like a lifeless thing; and that the soul, carried meanwhile far from the body, when the wand was brought near it again, after its entry reported every detail. Accordingly, from this both the other spectators of this kind of inquiry and Aristotle were convinced that the soul is separable from the body. This, then, which I am saying — that the soul can go out of the body and enter it again, and make what it had left breathe once more — is shown by these things written long ago by the leaders of the Peripatos; and whatever has been handed down by the theurgists of the time of Marcus provides clear proof of the account. For they too, by a certain rite, do the same thing to the person being initiated; and every such contrivance is not human but daemonic and divine. So it would be no wonder if, for the spectacles set before him, the man of good form, by [divine] will, both went out of the body while it remained uncorrupted, and, having gone out, gained a power able to behold things invisible to our senses, and memory of what he saw, and the telling of it; for this was no ordinary soul, but one that received this privilege from the gods because of its superiority to the other souls — in its very essence, if you like; or, if that is hard to accept, because of the godlike character of its life. For nothing prevents it from differing from them even in essence, and, as being nearer to the gods, from having [obtained] this direct vision; just as oracles too [have been] our teachers [about other] souls, which came from above, from higher chains and more sovereign orders, to reveal to the lower souls many of the divine goods, even of those beyond their grasp. But if anyone should say that this too is unclear, this at least is known to all: that the messenger of these things, having lived a present life surpassing that of his peers, must have shown himself worthy of this messenger's office towards those [souls]. For one can see how the participation in the gift bestowed by providence, beginning from above from the gods themselves, and the power that reveals divine things through intellect, sinking down little by little, proceed through the intermediate beings, among which the one next to the gods, being surely more like them than those further off, thus ferries across the truth that is established among them: this one first sees the divine things; after him, those to whom he announced them receive the self-manifest knowledge through hearing; then those after them, receiving it from them in turn, † the report of what they heard. And this is clear evidence of being further from or nearer to the divine apparitions themselves; and he who first of all had converse with them is surely more godlike than the others. For I would not ascribe even the good fortune of hearing these things to anyone without the good lot that comes down from the gods; so much the more, then, must the divine [vision] belong to a surpassing excellence of life that has risen to the summit.
